stem: In a 70-kg adult, Drug X has a Vd of 5 L and Drug Y has a Vd of 500 L. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Drug X is mostly in tissue, not plasma
options.B: Drug Y occupies a real 500-L body space
options.C: Vd shows which drug is more potent
options.D: Both drugs are mostly confined to plasma
options.E: Drug Y is mostly in tissue, not plasma

why: A high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution; it is a calculated, theoretical volume. Digoxin, with a Vd of about 500 L, is the classic example.

whys.A: A small Vd means the drug stays mostly in plasma.
whys.B: Vd is theoretical, not an anatomic space.
whys.C: Vd describes distribution, not potency.
whys.D: Y's very high Vd means extensive tissue distribution.

takeaway: High Vd = sequestered in tissue (digoxin ~500 L).
discriminator: Vd is math, not anatomy.

stem: After surgery, an inhaled anesthetic gas leaves the body mainly through which route?
why: Lungs eliminate volatile agents such as anesthetic gases.

whys.A: The kidney is dominant for MOST drugs, but not volatile gases.
whys.C: For some large or protein-bound drugs.
whys.D: A minor route.
whys.E: A minor route that matters in lactation.

takeaway: Volatile → lungs.
discriminator: Match the drug type to the route.

stem: A patient received an irreversible antagonist; its plasma level is now undetectable, yet the blockade persists for days. Why?

options.A: Recovery must wait for new receptor synthesis
options.B: Protein binding keeps the drug active
options.C: Its plasma half-life is several days
options.D: Competitive binding still holds the site
options.E: The drug slowly leaks back out of fat

why: An irreversible antagonist permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized, so its effect depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination.

whys.B: Bound drug isn't active.
whys.C: Its level is already gone.
whys.D: Irreversible, not competitive, binding.
whys.E: The plasma level is undetectable; the receptor itself is inactivated.

takeaway: Irreversible effect lasts as long as receptor turnover.
discriminator: Effect outlasting the drug → irreversible antagonist.

stem: A patient on lithium develops worsening chronic kidney disease. What is the safest plan?

options.A: Lower the dose or extend the interval and check levels
options.B: Raise the dose to maintain the effect
options.C: Stop monitoring since levels are predictable
options.D: Switch to IV lithium to bypass the kidney
options.E: Keep the dose, since lithium is liver-cleared

why: Renally cleared, narrow-TI drugs (lithium, digoxin, many antibiotics) need a dose or interval adjustment in renal impairment, guided by eGFR/CrCl, with blood levels.

whys.B: Exposure is already rising; a higher dose adds risk.
whys.C: Narrow-TI drugs need closer monitoring in CKD.
whys.D: Route doesn't change renal clearance.
whys.E: Lithium is renally cleared.

takeaway: CKD + renally cleared narrow-TI drug → adjust + monitor.
discriminator: Less clearance → more exposure.

stem: A drug has a Vd of 70 L and a clearance of 7 L/h. Using t½ = 0.7 × Vd ÷ CL, what is its half-life?
why: t½ = 0.7 × Vd ÷ CL = 0.7 × 70 ÷ 7 = 7 hours. Half-life rises when Vd rises or clearance falls.

whys.A: Check the arithmetic: 0.7 × 70 ÷ 7.
whys.C: That multiplies instead of dividing by clearance.
whys.D: That ignores clearance.
whys.E: That is Vd ÷ CL without the 0.7 factor.

takeaway: t½ ∝ Vd ÷ CL.
discriminator: Lower clearance (e.g., CKD) → longer half-life.

stem: A patient who is a CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizer is prescribed codeine. What is the main concern?

options.A: Too little morphine forms, so no pain relief
options.C: Codeine cannot be absorbed by mouth
options.D: Too much morphine forms, risking toxicity

why: CYP2D6 converts codeine to morphine (about 200× more potent); ultrarapid metabolizers make too much morphine. CPIC recommends an alternative analgesic for ultrarapid and poor metabolizers.

whys.A: That is the POOR metabolizer problem.
whys.B: TPMT relates to thiopurines.
whys.C: Absorption is not the issue.
whys.E: HLA alleles relate to hypersensitivity, not CYP2D6.

takeaway: UM → too much active drug; PM → too little.
discriminator: For a prodrug, faster activation = more effect and toxicity.

stem: Which statement describes Phase I metabolism?

options.A: It often creates or unmasks a reactive group
options.B: It makes a drug less water-soluble for storage
options.C: It is carried out mainly by TPMT
options.D: It attaches a polar group such as glucuronide
options.E: It always follows Phase II conjugation

why: Phase I (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; mainly CYP450) often creates or unmasks a reactive functional group; Phase II then attaches a polar group.

whys.B: Metabolism moves toward excretion.
whys.C: Phase I is mainly CYP450.
whys.D: That is Phase II conjugation.
whys.E: Phase I usually comes FIRST, but not always.

takeaway: Phase I unmasks; Phase II conjugates.
discriminator: 'Reactive group' → Phase I; 'polar group' → Phase II.

stem: A patient on digoxin has nausea and a level of 2.6 ng/mL (textbook target about 1 ng/mL; toxic above 2). What is the best interpretation?

options.A: The level is in the toxic range for a narrow-TI drug
options.B: Digoxin levels are not clinically useful
options.C: Nausea proves the drug is ineffective
options.D: The level is ideal; continue the same dose
options.E: The level is low; increase the dose

why: Digoxin is a classic narrow-TI drug (target ~1 ng/mL, toxic >2 ng/mL in the textbook table); small changes push it into toxicity, so levels are monitored.

whys.B: Narrow-TI drugs rely on blood levels.
whys.C: Symptoms plus a high level suggest toxicity.
whys.D: 2.6 ng/mL is above the 2 ng/mL toxic threshold.
whys.E: The level is high, not low.

takeaway: Narrow TI → monitor levels; know the toxic threshold.
discriminator: Level above the toxic cutoff + symptoms = toxicity.

stem: An older patient brings two bottles with different brand names; both list acetaminophen as the active ingredient. What is the best counseling step?

options.A: Assume the two brands are different drugs
options.B: Advise relabeling both by chemical name
options.C: Stop the store brand since brands differ
options.D: Name the shared generic and flag the duplicate
options.E: Reassure that OTC products are always safe

why: Counseling by generic name exposes a shared ingredient hidden under multiple brand names, preventing double-dosing.

whys.A: Different brand names can hide the SAME generic ingredient.
whys.B: Chemical names are rarely used clinically and won't help the patient.
whys.C: The problem is the duplicated ingredient, not which brand.
whys.E: Duplicate acetaminophen risks unintentional double-dosing.

takeaway: Generic names reveal duplicate therapy that brand names hide.
discriminator: Two brands + one generic = duplicate therapy.

stem: A patient on an oral contraceptive starts St. John's wort for low mood. What is the main risk?

options.A: No interaction, since it is an herbal product

why: St. John's wort induces CYP3A4, speeding metabolism of drugs such as oral contraceptives, warfarin, and cyclosporine — lowering their levels.

whys.A: Herbal products can cause major CYP interactions.
whys.B: St. John's wort is an INDUCER — levels fall.
whys.D: HLA reactions are genetic, not CYP-induced.
whys.E: The effect is on metabolism, not absorption.

takeaway: Inducer → substrate ↓ → therapeutic failure.
discriminator: Ask about herbal products before prescribing.

stem: A researcher studies why the same codeine dose relieves pain in one patient but not in their sibling, because of inherited enzyme differences. Which branch is this?
why: Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation shapes an individual's drug response (e.g., CYP2D6 and codeine).

whys.A: PD is what the drug does to the body, not genetic differences between people.
whys.C: PK covers ADME broadly; inherited variation in response is pharmacogenomics.
whys.D: Toxicology is the study of poisoning.
whys.E: Development is the discovery-to-approval pipeline.

takeaway: Genes → different response = pharmacogenomics.
discriminator: Look for 'inherited' or 'genetic' in the stem.

stem: In worsening CKD, a renally cleared drug's half-life rises from 6 to 12 hours. About how long will a new steady state take with regular dosing?

options.C: No change, since dose size is unchanged

why: Steady state takes about 4–5 half-lives: 4–5 × 12 h = 48–60 h. Clearance ↓ → t½ ↑ → time to steady state ↑ → accumulation risk.

whys.A: That uses the OLD half-life (4–5 × 6 h).
whys.B: That is one old half-life.
whys.C: Time to steady state depends on half-life, which doubled.
whys.E: That is just one new half-life.

takeaway: Time to steady state = 4–5 × the CURRENT half-life.
discriminator: When half-life changes, recompute the clock.
src: L02 S23; S28 (notes); S30; SG U1-R11

stem: A patient with HIV tests positive for HLA-B*57:01. What does this mean for abacavir?

options.C: Abacavir must be given IV only
options.E: Abacavir is safe at any dose

why: Abacavir is contraindicated in HLA-B*57:01-positive patients because of hypersensitivity — like HLA-B*58:01 with allopurinol.

whys.B: Absorption is not the concern.
whys.C: Route doesn't prevent the immune reaction.
whys.D: The allele predicts hypersensitivity, not low levels.
whys.E: HLA-B*57:01 positivity is a contraindication.

takeaway: HLA allele + specific drug = severe hypersensitivity → avoid.
discriminator: HLA-B*57:01 → abacavir; HLA-B*58:01 → allopurinol.

stem: How does protamine reverse heparin's anticoagulant effect?

options.A: It competes with heparin at its receptor
options.D: It induces enzymes that clear heparin

why: Positively charged protamine binds negatively charged heparin, neutralizing it — chemical antagonism needs no receptor.

whys.A: Heparin isn't blocked at a receptor; protamine binds it.
whys.B: No receptor is involved.
whys.D: Reversal is by direct binding, not metabolism.
whys.E: That is physiologic antagonism.

takeaway: Chemical antagonism = one drug binds the other.
discriminator: Same receptor = competitive; opposite receptors = physiologic; direct binding = chemical.

stem: On a quantal dose-response curve, what does ED₅₀ mean?

options.A: The dose that is toxic in 50% of subjects
options.B: The dose at which 50% of individuals respond
options.C: The dose that is lethal in 50% of animals
options.D: The dose giving 50% of one patient's Emax
options.E: The fraction of a dose that is absorbed

why: In quantal curves, ED₅₀ is the dose at which 50% of individuals show the specified effect (different from graded EC₅₀).

whys.A: That is TD₅₀.
whys.C: That is LD₅₀.
whys.D: That is the graded EC₅₀, a different measure.
whys.E: That is bioavailability.

takeaway: Quantal = % of people responding; graded = size of one response.
discriminator: ED₅₀ (people) vs. EC₅₀ (effect size).

stem: A patient needs slow, sustained systemic drug delivery through the skin over several days. Which route fits?
why: Transdermal: slow, sustained systemic absorption through the skin (and it avoids hepatic first-pass).

whys.A: Sublingual is rapid, not sustained over days.
whys.B: Inhaled gives a rapid local lung effect.
whys.D: Topical is for a LOCAL effect with minimal systemic absorption.
whys.E: IV is immediate, not slow through the skin.

takeaway: Skin + systemic = transdermal; skin + local = topical.
discriminator: 'Systemic' vs. 'local' separates transdermal from topical.

stem: A second drug displaces a highly protein-bound drug from plasma proteins. What does the textbook say usually happens?

options.A: Free drug rises briefly, then returns to baseline
options.B: Total drug level always rises permanently
options.C: Bound drug becomes the active fraction
options.D: Free drug stays high for as long as both are given

why: If unbound drug rises from displacement, its elimination increases, and after about four half-lives the unbound concentration returns to its previous value (if unbound clearance is unchanged).

whys.B: Elimination increases and levels re-equilibrate.
whys.C: Only FREE drug is active.
whys.D: Higher free drug is cleared faster, so it re-equilibrates.
whys.E: Usually it is not clinically important.

takeaway: Only free drug is active — and the body re-balances free drug.
discriminator: Displacement alone is rarely the cause of toxicity.

stem: After a brand's patent expires, how does a generic version usually win FDA approval?

options.B: An IND application for first human testing
options.C: A full new application with new Phase III trials
options.D: An abbreviated application with bioequivalence data
options.E: Orphan-drug designation for a rare disease

why: Generic manufacturers file an abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) showing bioequivalence; patents last 20 years.

whys.A: MedWatch collects adverse-event reports.
whys.B: An IND starts clinical trials of a new drug.
whys.C: Generics use an abbreviated application instead.
whys.E: Orphan status is for diseases with <200,000 US patients.

takeaway: Generic = ANDA + bioequivalence.
discriminator: New drug → IND then NDA; generic copy → ANDA.

stem: Before prescribing for a patient who is 10 weeks pregnant, which checklist item directly prompts the PA to reconsider the drug choice?

options.A: The drug's brand and generic names
options.B: Indication — is there a reason to treat?

why: The checklist: indication; contraindications and allergies; renal and hepatic function; drug interactions (incl. CYP450); age, pregnancy, and other patient-specific factors; correct dose, route, and monitoring.

whys.A: Names are not on the checklist.
whys.B: Indication asks whether to treat at all.
whys.D: Interactions concern other drugs, not pregnancy.
whys.E: Organ function is a separate checklist item.

takeaway: Memorize all six checklist items.
discriminator: Pregnancy lives under 'age, pregnancy, patient factors.'

stem: Some antimicrobials and gene therapies act on which drug target class?
why: Transporters & nucleic acids: carrier proteins; or DNA/RNA for some antimicrobials & gene therapies.

whys.A: Ion channels gate the flow of ions across membranes.
whys.C: Nuclear receptors are one receptor subtype.
whys.D: Transporters are carrier proteins.
whys.E: Drugs inhibit (or rarely activate) enzymes.

takeaway: Five classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids.
discriminator: DNA/RNA target → nucleic acids.

stem: Which narrow-TI drug is about 95% excreted unchanged in urine and essentially not protein-bound?
why: Lithium: ~95% urinary excretion, 0% protein binding, target ~0.7 mEq/L, toxic above 2 — renal function drives its dosing.

whys.A: Phenytoin is ~89% bound with saturable metabolism.
whys.B: Warfarin is ~99% protein-bound.
whys.C: Digoxin is ~67% urinary with a huge Vd.
whys.D: Propranolol is a first-pass drug, not a narrow-TI example.

takeaway: Lithium + kidney function = constant watch.
discriminator: Renally cleared + narrow TI → adjust in CKD.

stem: Which law first required proof of efficacy, not just safety, for new drugs (after the thalidomide disaster)?
why: The Kefauver-Harris Amendments (1962) required proof of efficacy as well as safety; thalidomide's birth defects spurred them.

whys.A: It gave incentives for rare-disease drugs.
whys.B: It decided which drugs need a prescription.
whys.D: It created abbreviated applications for generics.
whys.E: The 1938 act required proof of SAFETY.

takeaway: 1938 = safety; 1962 = efficacy.
discriminator: Thalidomide → Kefauver-Harris → efficacy.

stem: Paracelsus wrote that "the dose makes the poison." What does this mean?

options.A: Drugs become harmless at very high doses
options.B: Only true poisons can ever cause harm
options.C: Any substance can harm at the wrong dose
options.D: Harm depends mostly on the brand name
options.E: Toxins are always made in a laboratory

why: The textbook explains Paracelsus's point: any substance can be harmful if taken in the wrong dosage.

whys.A: Higher doses raise, not remove, the risk of harm.
whys.B: Even useful drugs harm at the wrong dose.
whys.D: Harm depends on dose, not on the name.
whys.E: Toxins are poisons of biologic origin.

takeaway: Dose, not the label 'drug' or 'poison', decides harm.
discriminator: Links to toxicity: harm as exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.

stem: A patient with angina is told to place nitroglycerin under the tongue rather than swallow it. Why?

options.A: Swallowed tablets cannot be absorbed at all
options.C: Sublingual dosing makes the drug more potent
options.E: Sublingual dosing avoids its large first-pass loss

why: Nitroglycerin has a large first-pass effect; sublingual absorption enters systemic veins directly, bypassing the portal vein and liver.

whys.A: Oral drugs are absorbed, then lose drug in the liver.
whys.B: The issue is too LITTLE reaching circulation.
whys.C: Route doesn't change potency.
whys.D: Half-life is set by clearance and Vd.

takeaway: Big first-pass drug → choose a route that skips the liver.
discriminator: Under the tongue = straight to systemic veins.

stem: Drug A has an EC₅₀ of 2 mg and reaches 60% of maximal response; Drug B has an EC₅₀ of 20 mg and reaches 100%. Which is true?

options.A: B is more potent; A is more efficacious
options.B: B is more potent and more efficacious
options.C: They are equal, since both relieve symptoms
options.D: A is more potent; B is more efficacious
options.E: A is more potent and more efficacious

why: Lower EC₅₀ = more potent (Drug A). Higher Emax = more efficacious (Drug B). Potency and efficacy are independent.

whys.A: Reversed on both counts.
whys.B: B's higher EC₅₀ means LESS potency.
whys.C: EC₅₀ and Emax both differ.
whys.E: A's lower Emax means LESS efficacy.

takeaway: Read EC₅₀ for potency and Emax for efficacy — separately.
discriminator: Efficacy matters more clinically: B can do more.

stem: An IV dose gives 200 mg/L; the half-life is 8 hours. What is the concentration at 24 hours?
why: 24 h ÷ 8 h = 3 half-lives: 200 × (1/2)³ = 25 mg/L (87.5% eliminated).

whys.A: That is at 8 hours (1 half-life).
whys.B: That is at 32 hours (4 half-lives).
whys.C: Concentrations halve; they don't fall by thirds.
whys.D: That is at 16 hours (2 half-lives).

discriminator: Count half-lives first, then halve each time.

stem: Which term describes an inactive precursor that the body converts into the active drug?
why: A prodrug is an inactive precursor converted to the active drug, usually by metabolism — one of the purposes of metabolism is to activate a prodrug.

whys.B: An antagonist blocks a receptor; it isn't a precursor.
whys.C: An active metabolite comes from an already-active drug and extends its effect.
whys.D: A generic is a bioequivalent copy, not an inactive precursor.
whys.E: A toxic metabolite (e.g., NAPQI) causes injury.

takeaway: Metabolism can turn a prodrug ON (e.g., codeine → morphine, clopidogrel → active metabolite).
discriminator: Inactive until metabolized = prodrug.

stem: Which renal process uses active transporters to move additional drug from blood into the tubule?
why: Tubular secretion: active transporters move additional drug from blood into the tubule.

whys.A: Filtration is size-based passage of free drug.
whys.B: Biliary excretion is not a renal process.
whys.C: Ion trapping blocks reabsorption by ionizing drug.
whys.E: Reabsorption moves drug back into the blood.

takeaway: Filter (size) · Secrete (transporters) · Reabsorb (lipophilic).
discriminator: 'Active transporters' → secretion.

stem: An oral dose of 100 mg delivers 40 mg unchanged to the systemic circulation. What is its bioavailability (F)?
why: F = fraction of an administered dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged = 40 mg ÷ 100 mg = 40%.

whys.A: F cannot exceed 100%.
whys.C: 60% is the fraction LOST.
whys.D: Only an IV dose is 100% by definition.
whys.E: Check the arithmetic: 40/100.

takeaway: F = amount reaching circulation ÷ dose given.
discriminator: Fraction reaching vs. fraction lost — read carefully.

stem: For which drugs does the textbook stress capacity-limited (saturable) elimination?
why: Capacity-limited elimination (clearance falls as concentration rises) matters for phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin; clearance has no fixed meaning for these drugs.

whys.A: These were route and receptor examples.
whys.B: These were first-pass examples.
whys.D: These are not the saturable examples given.
whys.E: These were pharmacogenomic examples.

takeaway: Saturable: phenytoin, ethanol, aspirin.
discriminator: Small dose increase → big level jump for phenytoin.

stem: A patient on propranolol has a well-controlled resting heart rate, but during hard exercise the rate rises markedly. What best explains this?

options.B: Propranolol acts as a full agonist in exercise
options.C: Propranolol is irreversible, so it wears off

why: With a competitive antagonist, the response depends on how much agonist competes: exercise-driven norepinephrine and epinephrine can overcome a fixed propranolol dose.

whys.A: Induction takes time and isn't the mechanism here.
whys.B: It is an antagonist.
whys.C: Propranolol is a COMPETITIVE β antagonist.
whys.D: Receptors aren't destroyed by exercise.

takeaway: Competitive blockade is surmountable — by drug OR by the body's own agonist.
discriminator: More agonist → competitive block overcome.

stem: A drug's volume of distribution is about 0.04 L/kg (about 2.8 L in a 70-kg adult). Where is it mostly found?
why: A drug restricted to the plasma has a Vd near the plasma volume, about 0.04 L/kg (2.8 L/70 kg); large protein molecules such as antibodies behave this way.

whys.A: Total body water is about 0.6 L/kg.
whys.B: Extracellular water is about 0.2 L/kg.
whys.C: Fat is about 0.2–0.35 L/kg, for highly lipid-soluble drugs.
whys.E: Tissue sequestration gives a very HIGH Vd (e.g., digoxin).

takeaway: Small Vd = stays in plasma; huge Vd = in tissues.
discriminator: Compare Vd to the body's real compartments.

stem: Which statement reflects the textbook's view of drug selectivity?

options.A: Each drug binds only one receptor type
options.B: Side effects occur only at toxic doses
options.C: No drug causes only a single specific effect
options.D: Selectivity is the same as efficacy
options.E: Potent drugs are always more selective

why: Drugs are selective rather than specific: no drug causes only a single effect, so 'side effects' are expected pharmacologic effects.

whys.A: Drugs bind more than one kind of receptor.
whys.B: Unwanted effects can occur at normal doses (ADRs).
whys.D: Efficacy is the maximal effect.
whys.E: Potency and selectivity are different properties.

takeaway: Selective, not specific.
discriminator: Expect more than one effect from every drug.

stem: A new cancer drug expected to be highly toxic enters its first human trial. According to the textbook, who is enrolled?

options.A: No humans, only animals, until approval
options.B: Healthy volunteers, as in usual Phase I
options.C: Thousands of patients at many sites
options.E: Volunteer patients who have the cancer

why: Phase I usually uses 20–100 healthy volunteers, but if significant toxicity is expected (e.g., cancer, AIDS), volunteer patients with the disease take part instead.

whys.A: Phase I is the first human testing.
whys.B: Usual Phase I uses healthy volunteers, but not when significant toxicity is expected.
whys.C: That describes Phase III.
whys.D: That describes Phase IV, after approval.

takeaway: Slides: Phase I = healthy volunteers. Textbook exception: very toxic drugs → patients.
discriminator: Expected toxicity changes who is in Phase I.

stem: For a patient with intermediate TPMT activity, how does CPIC guidance adjust a thiopurine such as azathioprine?

options.A: Give the standard dose without monitoring
options.B: Switch to codeine for the same purpose
options.C: Avoid all drugs metabolized by CYP3A4
options.D: Start at double the usual target dose
options.E: Start at about 30–70% of the target dose

why: TPMT intermediate activity: start at 30–70% of the target dose and titrate with close monitoring (e.g., white blood cell counts); deficient patients need a drastically reduced dose or an alternative.

whys.A: Intermediate activity needs reduced dosing and monitoring.
whys.B: Codeine is an opioid, not an immunosuppressant.
whys.C: TPMT is not a CYP enzyme.
whys.D: Low TPMT raises toxicity — lower, not higher.

takeaway: Less TPMT → less thiopurine.
discriminator: TPMT deficiency raises thiopurine toxicity risk.

stem: Before approval, a new drug is compared with standard care in 3,000 patients at 40 hospitals to confirm efficacy and watch for adverse effects. Which phase is this?
why: Phase III confirms efficacy and monitors adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients (textbook: usually thousands), often multi-site.

whys.B: Phase I is small-scale safety and dosing.
whys.C: Preclinical testing comes before any human trial.
whys.D: Phase IV happens AFTER approval.
whys.E: Phase II gives preliminary efficacy in a few hundred patients.

takeaway: Large, multi-site, pre-approval = Phase III.
discriminator: Before approval → III; after approval → IV.

stem: A patient on warfarin and a barbiturate (a CYP inducer) has the barbiturate stopped. What should the PA anticipate?

options.A: Warfarin levels fall, raising clot risk
options.B: Warfarin levels rise, raising bleeding risk
options.C: Warfarin becomes a prodrug once again
options.D: No change, since warfarin is renally cleared
options.E: The barbiturate's effect on CYP persists forever

why: Inducers raise warfarin dose needs; stopping the inducer reduces warfarin metabolism, raising plasma levels and causing bleeding.

whys.A: Stopping an inducer slows metabolism — levels RISE.
whys.C: Not a feature of warfarin.
whys.D: Warfarin is cleared by CYP metabolism.
whys.E: Induction fades after the inducer is stopped.

takeaway: Stopping an inducer acts like adding an inhibitor.
discriminator: Watch narrow-TI drugs whenever an interacting drug is STOPPED, too.

stem: A patient stable on digoxin starts a drug that inhibits P-glycoprotein (MDR1). What does the textbook predict?
why: P-glycoprotein (MDR1) pumps drugs out of cells; inhibiting it increases blood levels of digoxin — dangerous for a narrow-TI drug.

whys.A: Digoxin's large Vd reflects tissue uptake, unchanged here.
whys.B: TI is a drug property; the interaction raises toxicity risk.
whys.D: P-gp inhibition doesn't change how digoxin is activated.
whys.E: Blocking the efflux pump raises, not lowers, digoxin levels.

takeaway: Transporters cause interactions too, not only CYP enzymes.
discriminator: Efflux pump blocked → more drug stays in → level up.

stem: A patient overdoses on a weak base. Based on ion trapping, which urine change would speed its excretion?
why: Weak acids are excreted faster in alkaline urine; weak bases faster in acidic urine — the ionized form is trapped in the tubule and can't be reabsorbed.

whys.A: Changing pH is the ion-trapping strategy.
whys.B: Lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed.
whys.D: Alkaline urine speeds excretion of weak ACIDS (e.g., aspirin).
whys.E: Only free drug is filtered.

takeaway: Trap the ionized form: acid → alkaline urine; base → acidic urine.
discriminator: Aspirin (acid) → bicarbonate; a base → the opposite.

stem: Roughly what share of prescription drugs metabolized by the liver does CYP3A4 handle?
why: CYP3A4 alone metabolizes over 50% of the prescription drugs metabolized by the liver — why the lecture's interaction example uses CYP3A4.

whys.A: Many other enzymes are involved.
whys.B: Too low — that is closer to CYP2D6's share of all drugs.
whys.C: Far too low.
whys.D: Far too low.

takeaway: CYP3A4 = the busiest drug-metabolizing enzyme.
discriminator: CYP3A4 inhibitors and inducers affect many drugs.

stem: A PA is choosing a starting dose for an individual patient. According to the textbook, which range is most useful?

options.A: The range from EC₅₀ up to Emax
options.C: The range from LD₅₀ down to TD₅₀
options.D: The fraction of the dose absorbed

why: The therapeutic window — between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — is of greater practical value in choosing a dose for a patient.

whys.A: That describes potency and efficacy, not safety.
whys.B: TI is measured in animals; the window is more practical in a patient.
whys.C: Lethal-dose data come from animal studies.
whys.D: That is bioavailability.

takeaway: TI (animals) vs. therapeutic window (patients).
discriminator: Choosing a real patient's dose → therapeutic window.

stem: Why does a large acetaminophen overdose injure the liver?

options.B: Overdose induces CYP3A4 in the gut wall
options.C: The kidneys stop excreting the drug
options.D: Glutathione runs out, so NAPQI builds up
options.E: Acetaminophen itself is directly toxic at any dose

why: Most acetaminophen is conjugated; a small fraction becomes NAPQI, normally detoxified by glutathione. In overdose glutathione is depleted and NAPQI injures the liver; N-acetylcysteine within 8–16 h protects.

whys.A: NAPQI comes from CYP (Phase I) metabolism.
whys.B: Not the mechanism of injury.
whys.C: The injury is hepatic, from NAPQI.
whys.E: Toxicity comes from the NAPQI metabolite.

takeaway: Toxic metabolite + depleted defense = liver injury.
discriminator: NAPQI is made normally; overdose overwhelms glutathione.

stem: What does the textbook mean by "spare receptors"?

options.A: New receptors made after long-term use
options.B: Receptors that bind only antagonist drugs
options.D: Maximal response occurs without full receptor occupancy
options.E: Receptors that cannot bind any drug at all

why: Receptors are 'spare' when a maximal response can be produced without occupying all of them (e.g., ~90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response preserved).

whys.A: Spareness isn't about new synthesis.
whys.B: They bind agonists normally.
whys.C: Irreversible binding is a different concept.
whys.E: Spare receptors are functional receptors.

takeaway: Spare receptors = reserve capacity.
discriminator: Full response at partial occupancy → spare receptors.

stem: Which efflux transporter is found in the brain and testes and limits drug entry there?
why: P-glycoprotein (MDR1), an ABC efflux transporter in the brain, testes, and other tissues, pumps drugs back out.

whys.A: CYP3A4 is a metabolizing enzyme.
whys.C: TPMT metabolizes thiopurines.
whys.D: VKORC1 is the warfarin target gene.
whys.E: Albumin binds drug in plasma.

takeaway: P-gp = efflux pump at the BBB (and testes).
discriminator: Pumps move drugs; enzymes change drugs.

stem: Which route has a bioavailability of about 30% to <100% and less first-pass effect than oral dosing?
why: Rectal (PR): 30% to <100%, less first-pass effect than oral — about half of a rectal dose bypasses the liver.

whys.B: Transdermal is about 80% to ≤100% and very slow.
whys.C: Inhalation is 5% to <100% with very rapid onset.
whys.D: IM is about 75% to ≤100%.
whys.E: IV is 100%.

takeaway: Rectal partly avoids first-pass; sublingual largely avoids it.
discriminator: Not every non-oral route fully escapes the liver.

stem: A drug lowers blood pressure, whether or not that was the reason it was given. What is this measurable change called?
why: Pharmacologic effect = any measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).

whys.A: Toxicity is harm above the therapeutic range.
whys.B: Efficacy is the maximal effect (Emax) a drug can produce.
whys.C: An ADR is unintended AND harmful at normal doses.
whys.D: Therapeutic = the INTENDED, beneficial effect for a condition.

takeaway: Pharmacologic effect is the umbrella; therapeutic effect is the intended subset.
discriminator: 'Whether or not intended' → pharmacologic effect.

stem: Theophylline's Vd is 35 L, and the target level is 10 mg/L. Using loading dose = Vd × target, what loading dose is needed?
why: Loading dose = Vd × target concentration = 35 L × 10 mg/L = 350 mg — loading doses are based on Vd.

whys.B: Check the arithmetic: 35 × 10.
whys.C: That adds instead of multiplying.
whys.D: That leaves out the target concentration.
whys.E: Too large by a factor of ten.

takeaway: Loading → Vd; maintenance → clearance.
discriminator: Fill the volume to the target.

stem: A patient who drinks grapefruit juice daily has a higher level of a CYP3A4-substrate drug. What does the textbook say explains this?

options.C: Grapefruit binds the drug in the gut
options.D: Gut-wall CYP3A4 and P-gp are inhibited

why: Grapefruit juice inhibits P-glycoprotein and gut-wall CYP3A4 metabolism, which can substantially increase drug absorption — first-pass loss can happen in the gut wall as well as the liver.

whys.A: Not the mechanism described.
whys.B: Induction would LOWER the level.
whys.C: Binding would reduce absorption.
whys.E: Faster clearance would lower the level.

takeaway: First-pass happens in the gut wall too.
discriminator: Grapefruit = inhibitor (↑ levels), not inducer.

stem: Under FDA rules, how soon must an adverse event that is both serious and unexpected be reported?
why: Events that are both serious and unexpected must be reported to the FDA within 15 days.

whys.A: Not the stated deadline.
whys.C: Not the stated deadline.
whys.D: Not the stated deadline.
whys.E: Not the stated deadline.

takeaway: Serious + unexpected → 15 days.
discriminator: Postmarketing reporting is how rare effects surface.

stem: A patient with G6PD deficiency develops very high uric acid during cancer treatment. Which drug does the textbook say is contraindicated?
why: Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (risk of hemolytic anemia); an alternative such as allopurinol is used.

whys.A: Not the G6PD contraindication described.
whys.C: Allopurinol is the suggested alternative agent.
whys.D: Lithium is a narrow-TI renal drug, unrelated here.
whys.E: Albuterol is a β2 agonist, unrelated here.

takeaway: G6PD deficiency → avoid rasburicase.
discriminator: Genotype is one input — here it changes the drug choice.
